messages.content: If a,b belong to integer asqaure-4b is not equal to 2 prove it

# Proof (short and direct)

Assume \(a,b\in\mathbb{Z}\). Suppose for contradiction that
\[
a^2-4b=2.
\]
Rearrange to get
\[
4b=a^2-2,
\]
so \(a^2-2\) must be divisible by \(4\). That means
\[
a^2\equiv 2\pmod{4}.
\]

But an integer square modulo \(4\) can only be \(0\) or \(1\):
- If \(a\) is even, \(a=2k\Rightarrow a^2=4k^2\equiv0\pmod4\).
- If \(a\) is odd, \(a=2k+1\Rightarrow a^2=4k(k+1)+1\equiv1\pmod4\).

So \(a^2\) cannot be congruent to \(2\pmod4\). This contradicts \(a^2\equiv2\pmod4\). Therefore no integers \(a,b\) satisfy \(a^2-4b=2\).

QED.

Short trick: look modulo \(4\).

If \(a\) is even then \(a^2\equiv0\pmod4\), so \(a^2-4b\equiv0\pmod4\) — it can’t equal \(2\).
If \(a\) is odd then \(a^2\equiv1\pmod4\), so \(a^2-4b\equiv1\pmod4\) — again it can’t be \(2\).

Therefore \(a^2-4b=2\) has no integer solutions.

One-line version you can memorize: “an integer square is \(0\) or \(1\) mod \(4\), never \(2\).”  

Extra: same trick rules out any equation \(a^2-4b\equiv2\pmod4\); more generally, any congruence demanding a square be congruent to \(2\pmod4\) is impossible.
